archetypes.name: Electrically small circular loop
archetypes.summary: Single-turn circular loop with C < lambda/3, behaving as a magnetic dipole with essentially uniform current.
archetypes.notes: Radiation resistance uses the classic uniform-current magnetic-dipole result Rr = 20*pi^2*(C/lambda)^4 = 31171*(A/lambda^2)^2 (the two forms agree to 3e-6 because 320*pi^4 = 31170.909). The coefficient 20*pi^2 = 197.392 embeds eta = 120*pi; using the exact eta0 = 376.7303 gives 197.253, a 0.07% difference that is far below the accuracy of any other term, so the textbook coefficient is kept for test reproducibility. Against the exact uniform-current integral Rr = eta*(pi/2)*ka*Int(0,2ka){J2(x)dx}, the quartic law reads HIGH by +0.27% at C=0.1*lambda, +2.3% at C=lambda/3, +5.2% at C=lambda/2, +22.5% at C=lambda -- this is exactly why the validity limit is C < lambda/3. Loss resistance is the SKIN-EFFECT-LIMITED value for an isolated conductor; it is a LOWER bound (see proximity-effect caveat in validity). Inductance uses the high-frequency (surface-current) circular-loop formula L = mu0*a*(ln(8a/b) - 2); the low-frequency form uses -7/4 instead of -2 because it adds the internal inductance mu0*l/(8*pi). Efficiency of a practical small loop is usually a few percent or less; the number this spec returns is optimistic unless a realistic proximity factor is supplied.

synthesis.notes: Circumference follows directly from the chosen electrical size. C_over_lambda <= 1/3 keeps the quartic Rr law within 2.3%.
Loop radius a = C/(2*pi).

Wire radius needed to hit eta_target, from Rloss = Rr*(1/eta - 1) with Rloss = (N*C/(2*pi*b))*Rs. Inverts to b = N*C*Rs/(2*pi*Rr*(1/eta - 1)). Ignores proximity effect, so the real efficiency will be lower; for N>1 divide the resulting b by the expected proximity factor's square root or simply use the largest conductor that fits.
Loop self-inductance that must be series-resonated. 8*a/b = 4*C/(pi*b).

Series capacitance to resonate the loop at f0: C_tune = 1/(omega^2 * L). For a transmitting small loop this capacitor carries the full loop current and stands off V = I*X_C, which is typically kilovolts -- the capacitor, not the conductor, is usually the limiting component.

analysis.notes: Rr = 20*pi^2*(C/lambda)^4 = 31171*(A/lambda^2)^2. Uniform current assumed. Reads high by 2.3% at C=lambda/3.
Rs = sqrt(pi*f*mu/sigma) = 1/(sigma*delta). Copper: Rs = 2.6090e-7*sqrt(f) ohm.
delta = sqrt(1/(pi*f*mu*sigma)) = sqrt(2/(omega*mu*sigma)). Copper at 100 MHz: 6.61 um.

Rloss = (N*C/(2*pi*b))*Rs, i.e. conductor length divided by the effective conducting perimeter 2*pi*b, times the surface resistance. SKIN-EFFECT-LIMITED, isolated-conductor value only -- see validity for the proximity-effect multiplier and the b/delta floor.
Low-frequency limit. The skin-effect expression is only valid when b/delta > ~3; below that use max(Rdc, Rhf) or the exact Bessel form.
e_cd = Rr/(Rr + Rloss). Optimistic: excludes proximity effect, tuning-capacitor ESR and any ground/nearby-object loss.
D0 = 1.5 exactly (sin^2(theta) pattern, identical to a Hertzian dipole), i.e. 1.7609 dBi. Maximum lies IN the plane of the loop; there is a null on the loop axis.
G = e_cd * D0.
L = mu0*N^2*a*(ln(8a/b) - 2), high-frequency (surface current) circular-loop inductance. Accurate to ~2% for b/a < 0.1. Use -7/4 instead of -2 at DC.
Untuned terminal impedance: Zin = Rr + Rloss + j*omega*L. Strongly inductive; a series capacitor of C_tune cancels X.
Q = omega*L/(Rr + Rloss), the tuned (series-resonant) loop Q. Ignores capacitor ESR, which often dominates in a real transmitting loop.
Half-power fractional bandwidth = 1/Q.
FBW(VSWR<=s) = (s-1)/(Q*sqrt(s)) for a matched, singly-tuned antenna (Yaghjian & Best 2005). s=2 gives 0.7071/Q.

Chu-McLean lower bound Q_lb = 1/(ka)^3 + 1/(ka) for a lossless antenna in a sphere of radius a; here ka = C/lambda. A lossy antenna can go below this as Q >= e_cd*Q_lb, so the useful check is quality_factor >= radiation_efficiency * chu_limit_q.
Ae = G*lambda^2/(4*pi). For receiving use with the externally-noise-limited argument in the ferrite archetype.

validity: C < lambda/3 (ka < 0.333) -- beyond this the quartic Rr law over-predicts (+5.2% at C=lambda/2, +22.5% at C=lambda)
uniform current around the loop, which requires C << lambda and a loop whose feed/tuning gap is small
thin wire, b/a < 0.1, and turns-free single conductor
skin-effect loss expression requires b/delta > ~3; below that use the DC or exact-Bessel resistance

PROXIMITY EFFECT: for a single isolated turn the given Rloss is correct; whenever conductors are near each other (N>1, or a loop close to a ground plane/shield) the true loss is Rloss*(1 + Rp/R0) with Rp/R0 typically 0.5-4 (Balanis Fig. 5-9). This spec returns the Rp/R0 = 0 value
free space; a real loop near ground or lossy dielectric loses far more than Rloss predicts
excludes tuning-capacitor ESR, solder-joint and connector resistance, which often exceed the conductor loss in a high-Q transmitting loop

Validity-edge check: exact uniform-current integral gives 2.3817 ohm, so the quartic law is +2.3% here

archetypes.name: Electrically small square loop
archetypes.summary: Single-turn square loop of side s with perimeter < lambda/3; same magnetic-dipole physics as the circular loop but with a smaller enclosed area for a given conductor length.
archetypes.notes: The small-loop result depends only on the ENCLOSED AREA, not the shape: Rr = 31171*(A/lambda^2)^2 with A = s^2. Written against the perimeter P = 4s this becomes Rr = 121.76*(P/lambda)^4, i.e. (pi/4)^2 = 0.6169 times the circular value for the same conductor length -- the circle is the best small loop per metre of wire. The inductance constant -0.77401 is exact for a square of round wire at HF and is derivable from partial inductances: L = 4*(Lp - M) with Lp = (mu0*s/2pi)*(ln(2s/b)-1) and M = (mu0*s/2pi)*(ln(1+sqrt2) - sqrt2 + 1), giving L = (2*mu0*s/pi)*(ln(s/b) + ln2 - 1 - (ln(1+sqrt2) - sqrt2 + 1)) = (2*mu0*s/pi)*(ln(s/b) - 0.774013). Add mu0*s/(2*pi) (i.e. +0.25 inside the bracket) for the DC/low-frequency value. Corner current crowding adds a few percent of extra loss that this spec does not model.

archetypes.name: Multi-turn electrically small loop
archetypes.summary: N-turn air-core small loop; radiation resistance rises as N^2 while loss rises roughly as N, so multi-turn loops trade bandwidth for a usable feed impedance.
archetypes.notes: Rr scales as N^2 exactly (the N turns are coincident magnetic dipoles adding in phase, so the magnetic moment is N*I*A). Loss resistance scales as N to first order because the conductor length scales as N -- BUT the proximity effect between adjacent turns makes the true loss grow faster. Balanis writes Rohmic = (N*a/b)*Rs*(Rp/R0 + 1), where Rp/R0 is a measured proximity factor (Balanis Fig. 5-9) that depends on the turn spacing/wire-diameter ratio and on N; it is 0 for an isolated turn and typically 0.5-4 for a tightly wound multi-turn loop. This spec exposes Rp_ratio as an explicit input with a conservative default of 1.0 rather than pretending the skin-effect value is the answer. Set Rp_ratio = 0 to reproduce the textbook skin-effect-only figure. Inductance is given in two forms: bunched (all turns effectively coincident, L = N^2 * single-turn L, an UPPER bound) and Wheeler's current-sheet solenoid formula (better whenever l_coil > 0.8*a; accurate to ~1% there). Wheeler's SI form L = mu0*N^2*pi*a^2/(l + 0.9*a) is identical to the classic L[uH] = a^2*N^2/(9a + 10l) with a, l in inches to within 0.3%. Self-resonance from inter-turn capacitance is NOT modelled and is the practical ceiling on N.

The most radiation resistance a winding of this turn size can have while its whole wire stays within the limit: a multi-turn small loop cannot reach tens of ohms.

Rohmic = (N*C/(2*pi*b))*Rs*(1 + Rp/R0). Use Rp_ratio from Balanis Fig. 5-9 or from measurement.
e_cd = Rr/(Rr + Rohmic), with the proximity factor included.
D0 = 1.5 (1.7609 dBi); unchanged by N as long as the winding stays electrically small.
G = e_cd*D0.
The winding's inductance from the coaxial-ring model (see L_tune); what the impedance, Q and tuning use.

Upper bound for turns bunched into a bundle of effective radius b: L = N^2*mu0*a*(ln(8a/b) - 2). Real windings fall between this and the Wheeler value.

Q = omega*L/(Rr + Rohmic). Higher N raises both L (as N^2) and R (as ~N), so Q rises roughly as N -- multi-turn loops are narrower, not wider.

archetypes.name: Ferrite-rod loaded receiving loop
archetypes.summary: Multi-turn coil on a ferrite rod, used as an electrically tiny receiving antenna at LF/MF/HF where its dreadful efficiency is irrelevant because external noise dominates.
archetypes.notes: THE CRITICAL POINT: the useful permeability is the ROD permeability mu_rod, not the material's initial permeability mu_i. A finite rod demagnetises itself, and mu_rod = mu_i / (1 + D*(mu_i - 1)) where D is the demagnetising factor set by the rod's LENGTH/DIAMETER RATIO m = l_rod/d_rod. As mu_i -> infinity, mu_rod -> 1/D: the rod saturates at a geometry-determined ceiling. Worked ceilings (prolate-spheroid D): m=5 -> 17.9, m=10 -> 49.3, m=20 -> 148.2, m=50 -> 693. So a 10:1 rod of mu_i = 125 material gives mu_rod = 35.6 while the same rod of mu_i = 2000 material gives only 48.1 -- a 16x change in mu_i buys 1.35x in mu_rod. Using mu_i directly is the single most common error in ferrite-rod antenna calculations and over-predicts signal voltage by one to two orders of magnitude. D here is the EXACT prolate-spheroid (ellipsoid of revolution) value, D = (1/(m^2-1))*((m/sqrt(m^2-1))*ln(m + sqrt(m^2-1)) - 1); the large-m limit is (ln(2m)-1)/m^2. CONFIDENCE IS LOW on mu_rod's absolute accuracy because real rods are CYLINDERS, not spheroids: measured cylinder demagnetising factors (Bozorth & Chapin) run roughly 10-20% below the equivalent-spheroid value (e.g. m=10: D_cyl ~ 0.017 vs D_spheroid = 0.0203), so this spec UNDER-estimates mu_rod by of order 10-20%. The D expression itself is exact and is tested tightly; the physical mapping to a cylinder is the uncertain step. SECOND EMPIRICAL STEP: a coil shorter than the rod does not see the full mu_rod. k_coil (Snelling's coil-length correction, ~0.4 for a very short centred coil to ~1.0 for a coil covering the rod) is an empirical input with a default of 0.7, not a prediction. Ferrite loss (mu''), not copper loss, usually sets Q above a few hundred kHz; MnZn materials are unusable above ~2 MHz and NiZn above ~30 MHz. Do NOT use this archetype for transmitting: rod flux density saturates and the core heats.

parameters.name: target_length_diameter_ratio
parameters.description: Desired rod length/diameter ratio for synthesis

parameters.name: target_inductance
parameters.description: Coil inductance required to resonate with the chosen tuning capacitor

synthesis.notes: Rod length from the target aspect ratio. Longer rods win: mu_rod rises roughly as m^2/(ln(2m)-1).
Rod (apparent) permeability from the demagnetising factor. Depends on l_rod/d_rod, NOT on mu_i alone. Saturates at 1/D for large mu_i.
Permeability the coil actually sees, mu_eff = k_coil*mu_rod. k_coil is empirical (Snelling coil-length chart).

Turns for a target inductance, from the solenoid-on-core relation L = mu0*mu_eff*N^2*A_rod/l_coil. Round to an integer and re-check L. Accurate only to ~20% -- always trim the winding against a measured L or against the tuning capacitor.
Parallel tuning capacitance, C = 1/(omega^2*L). Add stray and varactor capacitance before choosing the gang.

analysis.notes: Prolate-spheroid demagnetising factor along the rod axis, D = (1/(m^2-1))*((m/sqrt(m^2-1))*arccosh(m) - 1) with m = l_rod/d_rod. EXACT for a spheroid; a real cylinder measures roughly 10-20% lower.
Large-m simplification D ~ (ln(2m)-1)/(m^2-1); within 0.7% of the exact value for m >= 10.
mu_rod = mu_i/(1 + D*(mu_i - 1)). THE FORMULA THAT MATTERS. Ceiling 1/D is independent of mu_i.
1/D, the largest rod permeability obtainable from this geometry no matter how high mu_i is.
mu_eff = k_coil*mu_rod, the flux-concentration factor seen by the winding. k_coil is empirical.

h_eff = 2*pi*N*A_rod*mu_eff/lambda. Open-circuit EMF for an incident field E (V/m) arriving in the loop plane is V_oc = h_eff*E; after tuning, the voltage across the tank is Q_coil*h_eff*E. Typical MF rod: h_eff of a few mm.
Rr = 31171*N^2*mu_eff^2*(A_rod/lambda^2)^2 (Balanis eq. 5-25a). Typically 1e-7 ohm or less at MF -- the antenna radiates essentially nothing, which is fine for reception.
L = mu0*mu_eff*N^2*A_rod/l_coil. Solenoid-on-core approximation, ~20% accurate; measure and trim.
Equivalent series loss R = omega*L/Q_coil, lumping copper loss, ferrite hysteresis/eddy loss (mu'') and dielectric loss into the measured coil Q. Above ~1 MHz on MnZn material, mu'' dominates.

e_cd = Rr/(Rr + R_loss). Expect 1e-7 to 1e-9 (-70 to -90 dB) at MF. This is NOT a defect: at LF/MF the external atmospheric and man-made noise floor is 40-80 dB above kTB, so the receiver stays externally-noise-limited even with this efficiency.
D0 = 1.5 (1.7609 dBi). The pattern is the small-loop figure-of-eight with deep nulls OFF THE ROD ENDS -- the rod is broadside-sensitive, which is what gives the classic AM-radio nulling behaviour.
G = e_cd*D0, a large negative number. Use effective_height_m, not gain, to predict receive performance.
The tuned-circuit bandwidth is set by the loaded Q of the tank, dominated by ferrite loss and by the detector/amplifier loading, not by radiation.

validity: RECEIVING ONLY -- core saturation and heating rule out transmitting at anything but milliwatt levels
l_rod/d_rod > 2 (the demagnetising expression has a removable singularity at m = 1 and is meaningless below it)
material frequency ceiling: MnZn (mu_i 800-5000) to ~2 MHz; NiZn (mu_i 40-800) to ~30 MHz. Above the ceiling mu'' collapses Q
mu_rod is a SPHEROID result applied to a cylinder -- expect it to read 10-20% low
k_coil is an empirical input, not a prediction
rod electrically tiny (l_rod << lambda), which is automatic at LF/MF
small-signal only: mu_i is field-dependent and the numbers here assume B well below the material knee
inductance formula ignores winding position along the rod; a coil at the rod centre sees more flux than one near an end

archetypes.name: Resonant one-wavelength circular loop
archetypes.summary: Full-wave circular loop with a cosinusoidal current; radiates broadside to the loop plane at about 3.6-3.7 dBi into roughly 140 ohm, resonating a few percent above one wavelength.
archetypes.notes: A one-wavelength loop is a completely different animal from a small loop: the current is NOT uniform but approximately cosinusoidal, the pattern maximum flips from IN the loop plane to NORMAL to it, and the feed impedance is a usable resistive value instead of milliohms. The pattern flip happens near C ~ 0.5*lambda. Do NOT apply the uniform-current (Alford) formulas here -- they would give D = 1.42 (1.53 dBi) with the maximum in the wrong plane. Resonance (X_in = 0) occurs at C ~ 1.09*lambda for a thin wire; the loop must be made LONGER than one wavelength, the opposite of the dipole's 0.47*lambda shortening. The exact resonant circumference depends on the thickness parameter Omega = 2*ln(2*pi*C/b) (King's loop theory, reproduced in Balanis Figs. 5-19/5-20): C_res/lambda falls from ~1.09 for very thin wire (Omega ~ 15-20) toward ~1.05 for fat conductors (Omega ~ 8-10). The engine uses 1.09; expect 1-4% trimming on a real build, and use the wire-thickness expression provided as a first correction. Rin ~ 100 ohm at that resonance is likewise a thin-wire figure that ranges roughly 80-130 ohm over practical conductor sizes. D ~ 3.4 dBi is the standard engineering figure (about 1.3 dB over a half-wave dipole); published values run 3.1-3.7 dBi depending on the assumed current distribution and conductor thickness. Bandwidth is estimated from a typical measured Q and is the weakest number here.

archetypes.name: Resonant square loop (quad element)
archetypes.summary: Full-wave square loop fed at the centre of one side, the driven element of a cubical quad. In free space it resonates at 1.05-1.14 lambda depending on wire gauge, into 124-140 ohm, with 3.27-3.49 dBi broadside.

Feed resistance of a free-space square quad loop is commonly measured at 100-130 ohm; 120 ohm is used here with a 25% tolerance. Gain is ~3.1-3.5 dBi; the square is very slightly worse than the circle because it encloses less area for the same perimeter. Bandwidth again rests on an assumed Q.

archetypes.name: Halo (bent half-wave dipole loop)
archetypes.summary: A half-wave dipole bent into a near-circle with a gap opposite the feed: purely horizontal polarisation round the horizon, about 1.2 dBi at the peak, and 2.7-3.3 dB of azimuth ripple - less omnidirectional than a halo is usually sold as.
archetypes.notes: A halo is NOT a loop antenna in the radiating sense -- it is a half-wave dipole rolled into a circle. Its circumference is about HALF a wavelength, not one wavelength, and the gap at the far end from the feed is a capacitive end-load that tunes it. Because the two halves are bent toward each other, their currents partially cancel: the radiation resistance falls to roughly 10-25 ohm (against 73 ohm for a straight dipole) and the pattern flattens toward omnidirectional in the plane of the ring, with a typical 1-2 dB azimuth ripple. GEOMETRY IS THE RELIABLE PART: total conductor length ~0.46-0.48*lambda, mean ring diameter ~0.5*lambda/pi = 0.159*lambda. That predicts a 2 m (146 MHz) halo 12.9 inches across and a 6 m (50.1 MHz) halo 37.5 inches across, both matching commercial products. EVERYTHING ELECTRICAL IS LOW CONFIDENCE: feed resistance, gain and bandwidth all depend strongly on the gap capacitance, the gap-plate geometry and the matching scheme (gamma, hairpin/beta, or folded conductor). The 15 ohm figure here is a mid-range value from published NEC studies and carries a 60% tolerance. A FOLDED halo (two parallel conductors, the outer one broken at the gap) steps the feed impedance up by the usual folded-dipole factor of about 4 for equal-diameter conductors, landing near 50-60 ohm, which is why most modern commercial halos are folded. Any real build must be modelled or trimmed; do not treat these electrical numbers as design values.

archetypes.name: Alford loop (uniform-current loop)
archetypes.summary: A square loop, typically 0.5-1.0 lambda in perimeter, with folded/capacitively-loaded corner sections that force the current to stay uniform and in phase, giving a horizontally polarised omnidirectional pattern with a usable feed impedance.
archetypes.notes: The Alford loop's defining trick is FORCING UNIFORM IN-PHASE CURRENT around a loop that is no longer electrically small. That means the small-loop pattern (D = 1.5, omnidirectional in the loop plane, nulls on the axis) is retained while the loop is big enough to have a sane radiation resistance. The correct analysis is therefore the EXACT uniform-current circular-loop solution, not the quartic small-loop approximation: Rr = eta*(pi/2)*ka*Int(0,2ka){J2(x) dx} and D0 = 2*ka*J1(ka)^2 / Int(0,2ka){J2(x) dx}, valid for 0 < ka < 1.8412 where the maximum stays in the loop plane (Balanis eqs. 5-33, 5-34b). Above ka = 1.8412 (J1's first maximum) the beam tilts off the plane and the antenna stops being omnidirectional in the useful sense. Both Bessel quantities are evaluated here as truncated power series (8 terms), which reproduce scipy's jv to better than 1e-10 over the whole valid range -- no numerical solve is needed. A square Alford loop is mapped onto the equivalent circular loop by EQUAL ENCLOSED AREA, ka_eq = 2*sqrt(pi*A)*f0/c, which is the correct small-loop equivalence and stays within a few percent up to ka ~ 1. Directivity falls slowly with size: 1.500 (1.761 dBi) at ka -> 0, 1.481 at ka = 0.5, 1.422 (1.530 dBi) at ka = 1, 1.211 (0.830 dBi) at ka = 1.8412. Real Alford loops measure below these because the current is never perfectly uniform and the folded corner sections radiate a little cross-polarised energy; budget 0.5-1 dB. CONFIDENCE MEDIUM overall: the uniform-current physics is exact, but the mapping from a real folded-corner structure to an ideal uniform-current loop, and hence the achievable feed impedance, is a design-dependent approximation.

analysis.notes: ka of the equal-area circular loop, ka_eq = 2*sqrt(pi*A)*f0/c. For a square of perimeter P this is 0.88623*(P/lambda).

D0 = 2*ka*J1(ka)^2 / Int(0,2ka){J2 dx} (Balanis eq. 5-34b), maximum in the plane of the loop, valid for ka < 1.8412.
Ranges 1.761 dBi (ka -> 0) down to 0.830 dBi (ka = 1.8412). Subtract 0.5-1 dB for real corner-loaded structures.
Skin-effect loss over the perimeter 4*sqrt(A). Uniform current makes this expression exactly the right one here, unlike for a resonant loop.
e_cd = Rr/(Rr + Rloss). Because Rr is tens of ohms rather than milliohms, efficiency is typically >99%.
G = e_cd*D0.

INDICATIVE, and now known to be entirely an allowance for imperfect current forcing rather than a property of the shape. With the current actually uniform, a square loop's horizon pattern is flat to 0.010 dB at a 1.0 lambda perimeter and 0.001 dB at 0.5 - fifty times smaller than the 0.5 dB carried here. So all of this budget is how well the folded, capacitively loaded corners do their job, which this spec does not model and cannot predict. Computed by prescribing a uniform current on the actual square geometry.
Ae = D0*lambda^2/(4*pi), lossless.

ASSUMED Q, and unlike its three neighbours in this family it cannot be derived here. The other loops' bandwidths are now solved, but an Alford loop's is set by the corner loading network that forces the current uniform, and that network is not part of the geometry this spec describes. Stated as an assumption rather than quietly fitted.

feed impedance is set by the corner-loading and matching network, not by Rr alone -- Rr here is the radiation resistance referred to the uniform loop current
free space; horizontal polarisation requires a horizontal loop plane and at least ~0.25*lambda of clearance
